newsitem.title: USA: Glickman doesn't see China as net importer soon.
newsitem.headline: Glickman doesn't see China as net importer soon.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Department Secretary Dan Glickman said he does not expect China to become a major importer any time soon.

In a speech to the Council on Foreign Relations in New York City that was released in Washington Thursday, Glickman said the department's long-term forecast was that food demands would eventually exceed China's food production.

"But I wouldn't hold my breath for a permanent shift to large net imports any time soon," he said. "As long as China remains single-mindedly focused on growing grain, it can put off the inevitable for some time."
In February, a prominent U.S. grain group forecast China feedgrain imports would soar to 23.5 million tonnes in 2005 from a net 1.5 million tonnes in the current marketing year.

In the speech to the foreign policy group, Glickman also said USDA now believed that China's agricultural landbase has been about 40 to 50 percent underreported, but noted that did not change the department's long-term forecast.
Glickman said the U.S. has made a TCK protocol a deal breaker on China's accession to the World Trade Organization.

Last summer, China cancelled purchases of 1.4 million tonnes of U.S. wheat, worth over $250 million, based on the presence of the wheat disease TCK. The U.S. argued Chinese concerns were not scientifically justified.

"If China were in the WTO, we would have had the chance to challenge them on the scientific merits. Since they are not we have made a TCK protocol one of several deal breakers on China's WTO membership," the Agriculture Secretary said.
He also said there had been "real progress" made on letting Americans do business in China without going through a centralized government entity.
"China has agreed to let foreign grain traders deal directly with private importers once they are in the WTO," Glickman said in the speech.
